vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: what a witness says on the record, as a formal account of what happened
to make information known that somebody would rather keep quiet
the facts and documents that can be shown to support what somebody says
the way a situation finally ends, after everything has been decided

legally responsible for something that went wrong, whether or not you meant it
the act of breaking a rule, a promise or an agreement
a person who saw or heard what happened and can describe it

paras: A photographer licensed one image for the cover of a novel. The fee was small and it was paid on time, the contract was signed by everybody it needed to be signed by, and for eighteen months nothing went wrong. Clause 7.2 said, in eleven words, that the licence covered the hardback edition and no other. Nobody in the building read it. When the paperback came out in March and the e-book in September, the photographer found out from a bookshop window in a town she was passing through. That was the breach, and the striking thing about it is that no single person decided to commit it.

What the file actually held was thin. A signed licence with the clause in it, and one email the photographer had sent at eleven at night asking whether a paperback was planned, which nobody answered and which she had not kept. The only witness who had been in the room when the paperback was approved was the cover designer, and her testimony helped nobody: nine people had seen the file that morning and not one of them had opened the licence, because by then the cover had stopped being a decision and had become a fact. The house was liable. The designer, who had never signed anything, was not.

The mediation took an afternoon. The most useful ten minutes of it were spent on sentences about things that had not happened, because that is the only part of a dispute where nobody has to lose to speak honestly. If somebody had read clause 7.2, the paperback would not have carried the photograph. If the house had disclosed the second print run, she would have found out in March instead of two years later. As it turned out, she had never asked for the book to be withdrawn and had never wanted it: she was asserting a fee and a credit, and the credit was the part she would not compromise on. The outcome was a figure smaller than her lawyer had asked for and a line on the copyright page of every edition from then on. In hindsight, one phone call in March would have saved two years and most of the money.

listenings.text: I have said this to every new person we hire since. The licence covered the hardback and nothing else, and it said so in one line, and everybody in this building assumed that a cover licence covered the book, in every form the book would ever take. That assumption is not written down anywhere. It is just there, the way water is there. The paperback was approved on a Tuesday morning and nine people saw that file, and not one of them opened the licence, because by then the cover had stopped being a decision and had become a fact. You do not check a fact. What would I do differently? One thing, and it is boring. I would put the limits of every licence on the front page of the file, in a single line, in a place you cannot scroll past. Not in the contract. On the file. And I will tell you what I would not do, because it was the first thing three people suggested. Blaming the designer would have been easy, and it would have changed nothing, because she was never the person who signed it. If I had let that happen, I would have lost the only person in the room who actually knew what had gone on that morning.

There is one question I ask in every session, and I ask it in the same place: after both opening statements, and before anybody says a number. What would you have done differently? Not what went wrong, and not whose fault it was. What would you have done differently. It sounds soft and it is the hardest working question I have. Here is why it works. It is the only question in the room that nobody can lose. Saying what you would have done differently is not the same as saying you were wrong, and everybody in that room knows the difference, so they answer it honestly, often for the first time in two years. And once one side has said it out loud, the other side stops defending, because there is nothing left to defend against. What happens when somebody refuses? It happens, and I let it. I just note it, and I can tell you that side almost always ends up paying more. A room that has heard no regret has nothing to build a compromise out of. You cannot construct an agreement out of two people who are both still completely right.
